scenes.visual: Dark background. A clean warm slate-white schematic of one sympathetic neuron spans the full frame width: rounded cell body with an indigo-violet nucleus on the far left, a long thin axon stretching across the center, and a branched axon tip on the far right touching a target organ releasing tiny gold circles (NGF). Title 'Beating Diffusion: The Signaling Endosome' fades in cleanly at top center (size 36) and fades out before s01.

scenes.tts: A sympathetic neuron collects its survival signal at an axon tip centimeters from its nucleus. Why can't that signal diffuse home, and how does the cell move it instead? Its axon can be a thousand times longer than its cell body is wide.
scenes.caption: A sympathetic neuron collects its survival signal at an axon tip centimeters from its nucleus. Why can't that signal diffuse home, and how does the cell move it instead? Its axon can be a thousand times longer than its cell body is wide.
scenes.visual: Carry the same full-frame sympathetic neuron (labelled 'schematic'). Gold NGF circles drift gently from the target organ on the right onto the axon tip. A pulsing glowing arrow spans the full axon from the right tip to the indigo nucleus on the left, with a clean label 'centimeters'. A scale bracket briefly highlights the small cell body on the left ('~30 µm') compared with the stretched axon.
scenes.narration: A sympathetic neuron collects its survival signal at an axon tip centimeters from its nucleus. Why can't that signal diffuse home, and how does the cell move it instead? Its axon can be a thousand times longer than its cell body is wide.

scenes.tts: Diffusion time equals distance squared divided by twice the diffusion constant. For a protein in cytoplasm, twice that constant is about twenty square micrometers per second. Across a thirty micrometer cell body, thirty squared is nine hundred, and nine hundred over twenty is forty five seconds. Diffusion works fine there.
scenes.caption: Diffusion time equals distance squared divided by twice the diffusion constant. For a protein in cytoplasm, twice that constant is about 20 µm²/s. Across a 30 µm cell body, 30² is 900, and 900 ÷ 20 is 45 seconds. Diffusion works fine there.
scenes.visual: Keep the neuron across the upper third; lower two-thirds show a live computed diffusion panel. As the narrator speaks, the equation 't ≈ x² / 2D' appears large (size 34), then '2D = 20 µm²/s'. A small zoom inset of the 30 µm cell body shows gold particles diffusing quickly across it while the live arithmetic populates step by step: 'x = 30 µm → 30² = 900 → 900 / 20 = 45 s', with a short computed horizontal bar labelled '45 s'.
scenes.narration: Diffusion time equals distance squared divided by twice the diffusion constant. For a protein in cytoplasm, twice that constant is about 20 µm²/s. Across a 30 µm cell body, 30² is 900, and 900 ÷ 20 is 45 seconds. Diffusion works fine there.

scenes.tts: Now stretch that trip to one centimeter, or ten thousand micrometers. Ten thousand squared is one hundred million. One hundred million over twenty is five million seconds, about fifty eight days. A neuron waiting on survival genes cannot wait two months.
scenes.caption: Now stretch that trip to 1 cm, or 10,000 µm. 10,000² is 100,000,000. 100,000,000 ÷ 20 is 5,000,000 seconds, about 58 days. A neuron waiting on survival genes cannot wait two months.
scenes.visual: The same computed panel transforms smoothly as distance x stretches along the axon to '1 cm (10,000 µm)'. Each number appears as spoken: '10,000² = 100,000,000', then '/ 20 = 5,000,000 s', then '≈ 58 days'. The computed diffusion bar shoots across the full frame width in muted red-amber while gold dots near the right axon tip jitter randomly and barely make progress leftward. On the left, the indigo nucleus dims.
scenes.narration: Now stretch that trip to 1 cm, or 10,000 µm. 10,000² is 100,000,000. 100,000,000 ÷ 20 is 5,000,000 seconds, about 58 days. A neuron waiting on survival genes cannot wait two months.

scenes.tts: Yet the message does arrive. Place a sealed barrier between cell bodies and axon tips, keeping their fluids apart. Give nerve growth factor, or NGF, only to the far axons, and many cell bodies survive. Inside the nucleus, the gene switch Creb turns on.
scenes.caption: Yet the message does arrive. Place a sealed barrier between cell bodies and axon tips, keeping their fluids apart. Give nerve growth factor, or NGF, only to the far axons, and many cell bodies survive. Inside the nucleus, the gene switch CREB turns on.
scenes.visual: A vertical white-grey schematic divider drops cleanly across the middle of the same neuron, splitting the frame into 'Cell body chamber' (left, clear fluid, no gold NGF) and 'Axon chamber' (right, filled with drifting gold NGF circles); the axon passes underneath the seal. A directional pulse moves leftward inside the axon beneath the barrier. On the left, the cell body stays bright and the indigo nucleus lights up with the label 'CREB active'.
scenes.narration: Yet the message does arrive. Place a sealed barrier between cell bodies and axon tips, keeping their fluids apart. Give nerve growth factor, or NGF, only to the far axons, and many cell bodies survive. Inside the nucleus, the gene switch CREB turns on.

scenes.tts: So the signal travels inside the axon, backward toward the cell body. That backward trip is retrograde signaling. At the tip, NGF binds its receptor, track A, and the membrane pinches inward by endocytosis. Predict: once that vesicle closes, does track A's active kinase face into the vesicle or out?
scenes.caption: So the signal travels inside the axon, backward toward the cell body. That backward trip is retrograde signaling. At the tip, NGF binds its receptor, TrkA, and the membrane pinches inward by endocytosis. Predict: once that vesicle closes, does TrkA's active kinase face into the vesicle or out?
scenes.visual: Smooth camera zoom into the right axon tip (same colour map, 'schematic'). On the slate-white plasma membrane sit teal transmembrane bars (TrkA) with glowing magenta-pink catalytic tails inside the cytoplasm. Gold NGF circles bind the outer teal ends, and the membrane begins dimpling inward into a deep cup. Just before the neck pinches shut, freeze the pinch with a crisp question card at bottom: 'Does TrkA's active kinase face into the vesicle or out?'
scenes.narration: So the signal travels inside the axon, backward toward the cell body. That backward trip is retrograde signaling. At the tip, NGF binds its receptor, TrkA, and the membrane pinches inward by endocytosis. Predict: once that vesicle closes, does TrkA's active kinase face into the vesicle or out?

scenes.visual: Hold the zoomed axon tip with the dimpling membrane gently pulsing at its neck and the question card 'Does TrkA's active kinase face into the vesicle or out?' clearly visible at full contrast. A subtle 4.5-second progress bar glides quietly along the bottom edge.

scenes.tts: It faces out, into the cytoplasm, because the membrane folds inward like a pocket. That surprises students, since endocytosis sounds like swallowing everything whole. The side that faced outside now lines the vesicle. NGF stays trapped inside, still gripping track A. Its kinase stays in the cytoplasm, ready to phosphorylate partners.
scenes.caption: It faces out, into the cytoplasm, because the membrane folds inward like a pocket. That surprises students, since endocytosis sounds like swallowing everything whole. The side that faced outside now lines the vesicle. NGF stays trapped inside, still gripping TrkA. Its kinase stays in the cytoplasm, ready to phosphorylate partners.
scenes.visual: The question card clears and the membrane neck pinches completely shut, releasing a round vesicle into the axon cytoplasm. Keep the outer membrane lining colour consistent so viewers watch it become the inner lining of the bubble: gold NGF sits locked inside the lumen bound to teal TrkA, while the glowing magenta kinase tails protrude outward into the cytoplasm and spark small partner blocks nearby. Label: 'Signaling endosome'.
scenes.narration: It faces out, into the cytoplasm, because the membrane folds inward like a pocket. That surprises students, since endocytosis sounds like swallowing everything whole. The side that faced outside now lines the vesicle. NGF stays trapped inside, still gripping TrkA. Its kinase stays in the cytoplasm, ready to phosphorylate partners.

scenes.tts: Now it needs a road and an engine. Axonal microtubules are polarized tracks, with plus ends toward the tip and minus ends toward the cell body. Cargo kinesins walk outward toward plus ends. Cytoplasmic dynein, aided by dynactin, walks toward minus ends, hauling the signaling endosome home.
scenes.caption: Now it needs a road and an engine. Axonal microtubules are polarized tracks, with plus ends toward the tip and minus ends toward the cell body. Cargo kinesins walk outward toward plus ends. Cytoplasmic dynein, aided by dynactin, walks toward minus ends, hauling the signaling endosome home.
scenes.visual: Zoom smoothly back out to show the long axon interior containing steel-blue microtubule tracks marked with clear '-' chevrons on the left (cell body) and '+' chevrons on the right (tip). A muted orange kinesin motor steps rightward toward '+'. Then a bright emerald-green dynein motor with a small attached dynactin collar latches onto the glowing signaling endosome and walks steadily leftward toward '-'.
scenes.narration: Now it needs a road and an engine. Axonal microtubules are polarized tracks, with plus ends toward the tip and minus ends toward the cell body. Cargo kinesins walk outward toward plus ends. Cytoplasmic dynein, aided by dynactin, walks toward minus ends, hauling the signaling endosome home.

scenes.tts: Motor transport grows linearly: time is distance divided by speed. At about one micrometer per second, dynein covers ten thousand micrometers in ten thousand seconds, under three hours. Five million over ten thousand: the motor is five hundred times faster. In the leading model, arriving endosomes trigger survival genes.
scenes.caption: Motor transport grows linearly: time is distance divided by speed. At about 1 µm/s, dynein covers 10,000 µm in 10,000 seconds, under three hours. 5,000,000 ÷ 10,000: the motor is 500 times faster. In the leading model, arriving endosomes trigger survival genes.
scenes.visual: While emerald dynein carries the glowing endosome steadily leftward into the cell body, the computed comparison panel reappears beneath the axon. The equation 't = x / v' appears, then '10,000 µm ÷ 1 µm/s = 10,000 s (< 3 hr)'. A bright emerald bar sits next to the massive muted red-amber '58 days' diffusion bar, labelled '5,000,000 s ÷ 10,000 s = 500× faster' (appearing as spoken). As the endosome reaches the cell body, its magenta kinase signals the indigo nucleus, which glows warmly.
scenes.narration: Motor transport grows linearly: time is distance divided by speed. At about 1 µm/s, dynein covers 10,000 µm in 10,000 seconds, under three hours. 5,000,000 ÷ 10,000: the motor is 500 times faster. In the leading model, arriving endosomes trigger survival genes.

scenes.tts: When an axon spans centimeters, passive spreading takes months. By hauling active signaling endosomes along microtubules, dynein delivers the survival message in hours. In the leading model, that is how neurons beat axonal distance, though other retrograde routes remain open.
scenes.caption: When an axon spans centimeters, passive spreading takes months. By hauling active signaling endosomes along microtubules, dynein delivers the survival message in hours. In the leading model, that is how neurons beat axonal distance, though other retrograde routes remain open.
scenes.visual: Full-frame view of the same sympathetic neuron: emerald dynein smoothly carrying a stream of glowing gold-teal-magenta signaling endosomes leftward along steel-blue microtubules into the illuminated indigo cell body, while the computed '58 days vs < 3 hr' contrast fades softly to keep focus on the moving transport. Soft subtle hedge tag 'leading model' sits cleanly beside the neuron.
scenes.narration: When an axon spans centimeters, passive spreading takes months. By hauling active signaling endosomes along microtubules, dynein delivers the survival message in hours. In the leading model, that is how neurons beat axonal distance, though other retrograde routes remain open.

scenes.visual: Clean dark end card displaying one line only, centered in large crisp white text (size 38), with no subtitle or smaller line underneath: 'Over long axons, dynein carries active signaling endosomes where diffusion fails.'
